# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This is a strong follow-up, and it settles several questions the earlier documents left open. It brings in a second hours measure, registers the mediation test before seeing the outcomes, discloses the ended arm, and states clearly that the Halden subset is "survivors twice over." Its rebuttals of the comment and the meta-analysis are mostly sound. The finding that all four long-follow-up studies in the meta-analysis were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours confirms the weakness I noted in that review's duration claim.

The arithmetic checks out:

- **Varden, output per hour:** 0.966 / 0.88 gives +9.8% (timesheets) and 0.966 / 0.89 gives +8.5% (logs). The confidence intervals follow from the output interval divided by the hours ratio.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Meeting time:** the difference-in-differences cut is 3.3 hours, matching the nine-month cross-sectional gap.
- **Halden subset:** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 and 96.8 / 86.6 gives +11.8%.

The problems are in how a few results are framed, and in one control-group issue the report notices but doesn't follow through. Most important first:

## 1. The meeting audit in control offices biases the 24-month estimate

The "unplanned observation" is treated as a side note about whether gains are available without cutting hours. But two of the seven **control** offices cut meeting time in month 15 and raised their output per hour by about 4%. That raises the control baseline, which shrinks the measured treatment effect at 24 months.

So part of the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may come from controls improving rather than from treated offices fading. Two further points:

- **This is likely spillover from the trial.** The nine-month report publicised the meetings finding, and control offices are in the same county. If so, it is contamination, and should be named as such.
- **Needed:** a sensitivity analysis excluding the two offices, or ending their contribution at month 15. That would show how much of the apparent decay is really decay. If the gap narrows, the "fading" conclusion weakens. If it doesn't, the conclusion is strengthened.

The section also says control meeting time moved from 7.2 to 7.0 hours. If two of seven offices fell by 2.1 hours each, the other five must have risen by about 0.5 hours on average to net out at −0.2. That is possible, but worth confirming.

## 2. The Summary compares different measures to describe the decline

The Summary says the per-hour gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." The 12.5% is from timesheets and the 8.5% is from system logs. The body handles this correctly: the like-for-like comparison is 12.5% to 9.8% on timesheets, a fall of about a fifth to a quarter. The Summary mixes the two measures and so overstates the fall at about a third.

Also, the decline isn't statistically established. The nine-month and 24-month intervals overlap substantially (+6.9 to +18.4 against +4.6 to +15.2), and no test of the difference is reported. "Consistent with some fading" is fair. "The gain has declined," in the Summary, and "declined by about a quarter," in Section 5, both state it as established. Adding the contamination in point 1 makes it less certain still.

## 3. It's unclear what the system logs measure

Logs record "active log-in time on the county's case-management system." That captures time spent on cases, but probably not meetings, email, phone calls or training. This matters in two ways:

- **As a total-hours measure.** If logs capture only case-system time, they can't be compared directly with timesheets, which record all paid time. Calling them "the stricter measure" assumes they cover the same work.
- **For the mediation.** The two readings don't fit together. Treated offices cut meetings by about 3.3 hours while total timesheet hours fell by about 4.5. If logs exclude meetings, case-system time should have fallen by only about 1 hour (about 3%), not the 11% reported. If instead logs do somehow include meeting time, the "meetings" pathway is partly arithmetic: removing hours that produced no output raises output per hour directly.

Either way, the report should define exactly what the logs record. It should also say whether pre-period log data exist, which a difference-in-differences estimate requires. If they do, a nine-month log-based estimate could be computed for a true like-for-like comparison.

## 4. "Confirms" overstates the mediation result

The Summary says the registered test "confirms" that meetings account for 47% of the gain. Registering the test before the 24-month data were seen is good practice. But "confirms" overstates what it can show:

- **The meeting cuts weren't randomised.** Treated offices chose how much to cut, so the analysis depends on the assumption that nothing else drove both meeting cuts and productivity. The Limitations section acknowledges this, but the Summary doesn't reflect it.
- **It isn't an independent test.** The hypothesis came from the same seven treated offices in the first nine months, and those months are part of the 24-month data. It is a pre-specified test in the same sample, not a replication.
- **The intervals may be too narrow.** The "larger sample of office-months" still comprises 14 clusters, and office-months within an office aren't independent. An interval of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters. The report should state how standard errors were computed and whether they account for clustering.
- **The mediators overlap.** Fewer meetings may reduce fatigue, so the split between the two pathways depends on how the model handles their overlap.
- **Where the baseline data came from.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. This report gives baseline meeting hours of 7.4 and 7.2. If calendars were extracted retrospectively, say so.

"Supports" or "is consistent with" would be accurate; "confirms" is not.

## 5. The Halden reversions don't all fit the Summary's description

The Summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations." Two (hospitality and retail) cited coverage. The third is a **marketing agency** that cited client deadlines. That is discretionary work under the meta-analysis's coding. Grouping it under "client-facing" blurs the distinction the report otherwise relies on. Discretionary work with hard external deadlines can also fail, and that is a finding in itself.

Other points on the Halden subset:

- **Response bias.** 14 of the 23 organisations with records responded. The nine that didn't may be disproportionately ones that reverted, so the 3-of-14 reversion rate is likely an underestimate.
- **Baseline hours.** The 40.3-hour baseline is identical to the 27-organisation average in the Varga–Holm comment; the 17-organisation subset had 40.4. Is this the 11 organisations' own baseline? Are all 11 among those with time tracking?
- **Attrition.** R. Okafor, the Halden lead author, is a co-author here. The comment's most serious finding was that seven of nine withdrawals happened after the reduced schedule began, contrary to the working paper's account. This report addresses the comment's other claims but not that one. It is the natural place to confirm or correct the record.

## 6. Cost is reported for counters but not case-processing

The counter arm comes with a cost estimate (12% more staff, +9% cost per contact). Case-processing, the arm that continued, gets none. With full pay, output per employee at −3.4%, and staff still claiming time beyond the 30 scheduled hours, payroll cost per case closed probably rose by several percent. That is the figure the county needs for its decision, and the report should give it.

The counter estimate also needs its basis. If 12% more staff restores output to about 0.99 of baseline, payroll per contact rises roughly 13%. The +9% figure implies non-staff costs make up about 30% of total cost, which should be stated.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Overstating the comment's claim.** The report says the comment's extrapolation implied "the gain falling to zero by month ten." The comment extrapolated *energy* to baseline at around month ten and argued the remaining gain was novelty. The rebuttal stands, but the wording should match what the comment actually said.
- **Secondary outcomes** (appeal rates, sick days, resignations) still have no confidence intervals. The sick-days measure may still fall partly mechanically, depending on rota design, as I noted for the nine-month report.
- **Appeal rates.** The lag concern I raised at nine months is now resolved for decisions from the first nine months: 3.2% against 3.0% is reassuring.
- **Registration timing.** The protocol was filed at month 11, after the nine-month results were known. The report states this, which is good. The Summary could say so too.
- **Ending the counter arm** is a disclosed deviation from the registered design. The month 10–12 waiting times (7.3 against 4.0 minutes, now with a control comparison) are a clearer measure than the nine-month report's treated-only figures.

## Overall

On the three questions the follow-up set out to answer:

- **Persistence:** a per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists at 24 months under randomised assignment, record-based output and two hours measures. How much it has faded is uncertain, because the decline isn't statistically established and the control offices were partly contaminated.
- **Meetings:** the meetings pathway survives a pre-specified test, which justifies taking it seriously. It is not causal confirmation.
- **Unrecorded work:** logs show slightly more work than timesheets, but until the logs are defined it is unclear whether they measure total working time.

The report's corrections to the comment and the meta-analysis are justified. Before it is cited, the Summary should match the body on the comparison of measures, the strength of the decline and "confirms," and the control-office meeting audit should be analysed as a threat to the main estimate.
